title: SCAFFOLD: Self-Improving Web Agents via Recursive Parametric Skill Abstraction
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence
  [Submitted on 31 Aug 2026]
    Title:SCAFFOLD: Self-Improving Web Agents via Recursive Parametric Skill Abstraction
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Web agents need to navigate visually rich, long-horizon interfaces that change across sites, yet most previous agents still learn each task in isolation and discard the procedural knowledge they accumulate. Recent skill-augmented frameworks take an important first step, but they treat the skill library as a flat or two-tier prompt-side cache and offer no principled mechanism for compressing redundancy or composing skills recursively. We introduce \textsc{Scaffold}, a self-improving framework for visual web agents that (i) induces parametric, executable skills from successful trajectories under a multi-instance abstraction constraint, (ii) maintains a recursively composed hierarchy in which higher-level skills invoke lower-level ones, (iii) compacts the library via a minimum-description-length (MDL) criterion and behavioral equivalence checking, and (iv) periodically distills skill-augmented trajectories back into model weights to internalize the abstractions. Across WebArena, VisualWebArena, and a held-out split of Online-Mind2Web, \textsc{Scaffold} improves success rate by $11.1$--$17.2$ absolute points over the strongest skill-augmented baseline and shows monotonic gains across five self-improvement iterations without library collapse. We release the code and documents in the Github \href{this https URL}{repository}.

report.summary: SCAFFOLD lets visual web agents extract reusable, composable executable skills from past successes and distill them into model weights, lifting task success by up to 17 points.
report.background: Web agents must operate visually rich, long-horizon interfaces — booking flights, filling multi-page forms, comparing products — where the layout and flow change from site to site. Most agents still learn each task in isolation and throw away the procedural knowledge they accumulate, so every new site means starting over. Skill-augmented frameworks were a step forward, but they store skills as a flat or two-tier prompt-side cache: retrieval lists that grow unboundedly, contain redundancy, and cannot express one skill calling another. That leaves two problems unsolved — how to compress and compose skills, and how to make learned procedures permanent rather than parked in a context window. SCAFFOLD, a new arXiv paper, attacks both by making skills parametric, hierarchical, pruned, and periodically distilled back into the model's own weights, evaluated on three standard web-agent benchmarks.
key_points: Skills are learned as parametric, executable programs induced from successful trajectories under a multi-instance abstraction constraint. A candidate skill only survives if it works across several different task instances, which filters out overfit, site-specific hacks and keeps only genuinely reusable procedures.

The library is recursively composed: higher-level skills invoke lower-level ones, so an agent can build a 'checkout' routine out of 'find item', 'add to cart', and 'enter payment' primitives. This mirrors how humans stack habits and gives compositional generalization instead of a flat list of tricks.

Compaction uses a minimum-description-length criterion plus behavioral equivalence checking, so the library does not collapse under its own weight. Skills that do the same thing, or that fail to earn their description length, are merged or dropped, keeping retrieval fast and context budgets sane.

Periodically, skill-augmented trajectories are distilled back into model weights. Learned abstractions stop being an external prompt-time crutch and become internal capability, which is what makes the improvement loop genuinely self-improving rather than just better retrieval.

On WebArena, VisualWebArena, and a held-out Online-Mind2Web split, SCAFFOLD beats the strongest skill-augmented baseline by 11.1 to 17.2 absolute points, and gains increase monotonically across five self-improvement iterations with no library collapse. Code and documents are released.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this reframes agent progress as a compounding loop — induce, compose, compress, distill — rather than a race for bigger prompts or hand-written tool lists. It suggests capability can be grown after deployment, which changes how teams think about evaluation and versioning. Developers get a concrete recipe: log successful trajectories, abstract them into parameterized skills, prune aggressively, then fine-tune on the results; the hard parts become infrastructure for trajectory capture, sandboxed skill execution, and regression testing between iterations. Regular users should eventually see browser agents that handle multi-step errands more reliably and remember procedures across sessions. The caveats are real: results are benchmark-bound, distillation is compute-heavy, and a self-editing skill library needs safety checks so bad abstractions are not silently internalized.
report.tools: To follow up, start with the benchmarks used here: WebArena, VisualWebArena, and Online-Mind2Web, which give reproducible web-task environments. The paper's GitHub repository (linked from the arXiv abstract page) releases code and documents. For adjacent building blocks, look at browser-use and Playwright for browser control, Agent-E and OpenHands for open agent frameworks, LangGraph for orchestrating iterative loops, and Voyager-style skill libraries for the original abstraction-plus-library idea that SCAFFOLD extends.
